Shares of Oracle (NYSE:ORCL) have underperformed the broader market this year, dropping 33% as of this writing, but the company appears poised for a strong finish.

The artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure giant held its Investor Day on Oct. 28, and its shares surged 11% in a single session due to its impressive long-term outlook. Of course, Oracle has given back its gains amid the brutal market sell-off. However, the company sees impressive growth acceleration through fiscal 2030, which explains why investor confidence in Oracle stock is likely to improve.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Let's take a closer look at Oracle's guidance through fiscal 2030 and see why this stock is poised for a major turnaround.

Image source: Getty Images.

Oracle's Investor Day presentation has eased concerns about its balance sheet

The primary reason for Oracle's underperformance this year is its debt. It has been raising money through debt and equity issuance to fund the aggressive build-out of data centers that handle AI workloads. As a result, the company's free cash flow has declined sharply over the past year and a half.

ORCL Free Cash Flow data by YCharts

However, Oracle estimates that it will become free cash flow positive in the second half of fiscal 2028. What's more, the company predicts more than $30 billion in free cash flow in fiscal 2029. It is worth noting that when Oracle released its fiscal 2027 Q1 results in September (for the three months ended Aug. 31), the company pointed out that customers funded a significant majority of the new contracts it signed during the quarter.

The company has been asking customers to make prepayments or bring their own hardware. This strategy will ease pressure on its cash flow. Not surprisingly, Oracle's data center infrastructure investments for fiscal 2028 are fully funded, as it noted in the Investor Day presentation. What's more, Oracle expects to bring its net debt to adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) below 3.5x by fiscal 2029.

A company with a net debt-to-EBITDA ratio between 1 and 3 is considered capable of servicing its debt payments. So, Oracle's guidance about its free cash flow profile and the debt seems to have assuaged investors' concerns about the health of its balance sheet. Moreover, the company has maintained its long-term growth targets.

Oracle (ORCL) stock just gave investors a reason to pause before selling. After a brutal year for the shares, a fresh set of forecasts during its Investor Day event has reignited hopes that the company's expensive AI ambitions could deliver serious cash flow. Oracle stock jumped 10.73% on October 28, closing at $144.54, though it remained down roughly 26% year to date. The rebound is significant, but one good day does not erase the risks.

However, before completely giving up on Oracle, investors should consider answering these three questions.

1. Can Oracle Turn Its AI Spending Into the Revenue Growth It Is Promising?

At its latest Investor Day, management didn't hold back, unveiling a bold vision. Oracle projects that its annual revenue will surpass $225 billion by fiscal 2030, representing average annual growth of more than 35% from fiscal 2026 levels. The company also doubled down on its fiscal 2027 targets of at least $90 billion in revenue and adjusted earnings per share of $8.10, in line with the consensus estimates. While these are forecasts, they give investors a clear sense of how high Oracle is aiming.

The opportunity goes beyond simply renting computing power to AI companies. Oracle combines cloud infrastructure, enterprise databases, and business applications into a powerful ecosystem. This matters because companies developing AI tools rely on reliable data storage, stable database services, and dependable software to keep operations running efficiently. Oracle's leadership sees these businesses amplifying each other. AI workloads drive demand for cloud capacity and database services. Meanwhile, AI-powered applications unlock new opportunities to sell subscriptions and services. For investors, this paints a richer growth story than a wager on data centers alone.

Oracle's contracted business offers another bright spot. At Investor Day, management spotlighted a staggering $664 billion in remaining performance obligations, with over 90% tied to infrastructure. This figure, representing revenue already locked in but not yet recognized, points to healthy demand for Oracle's future services. Still, it is important not to confuse it with immediate revenue.

What happened?

A number of stocks fell in the afternoon session after underwhelming earnings reports from tech giants Amazon and Intel (after mediocre earnings reports from Alphabet and ServiceNow the previous day) sparked widespread investor anxiety regarding aggressive artificial intelligence spending and sustained cash burn.

As reported by CNBC, disappointing quarterly reports from both companies triggered a broad slide across technology equities and hardware suppliers, overshadowing positive momentum in other areas of the market. Investors grew increasingly wary of the sector's rising capital expenditures—the funds poured into long-term assets such as data centers and computing hardware.

With both firms spending heavily to build out artificial intelligence infrastructure, market participants are questioning when these massive investments will translate into meaningful revenue and profit growth per CNBC. The steep drops in Amazon and Intel weighed heavily on market indices, showing how vulnerabilities among dominant technology leaders can rapidly dampen confidence across the broader industry.

IBM vs. ServiceNow: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

Investors seeking stability often look toward established tech giants, while those chasing growth prefer cloud-native leaders. Choosing between International Business Machines (NYSE:IBM) and ServiceNow Inc. (NYSE:NOW) requires weighing legacy strength against modern expansion.

International Business Machines focuses on hybrid cloud and AI consulting, making it a cornerstone for large enterprise modernization. Conversely, ServiceNow specializes in digital workflow automation, helping companies streamline complex internal processes. Comparing these two reveals how different software models approach the digital transformation market in 2026.

The case for International Business Machines

International Business Machines provides enterprise technology through its hybrid cloud and AI platforms. The company maintains a broad ecosystem of partners to deliver these solutions, including Adobe Inc. (NASDAQ:ADBE), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Oracle Corp. (NYSE:ORCL), Palo Alto Networks (NASDAQ:PANW), Salesforce.com Inc. (NYSE:CRM), Samsung Electronics (OTC:SSNLF), and SAP Inc. (NYSE:SAP). In October 2026, it launched 'IBM Ready for SAP Solutions' to assist midsize businesses with ERP modernization.

In FY 2025, revenue reached about $67.5 billion, marking a 7.6% increase from the prior year. Net income grew to approximately $10.6 billion, representing a net margin of 15.7%. This improvement suggests that the strategic shift toward high-value software and consulting is yielding financial results. As disclosed in its latest annual report, the company services thousands of organizations across more than 175 countries.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is 2.1x. This ratio compares total debt to shareholder equity, indicating the extent to which a company relies on borrowing to fund operations. The current ratio, which measures the ability to cover short-term debts with short-term assets, is roughly 0.9x. Free cash flow reached approximately $12.1 billion, which represents cash from operations minus capital expenditures.

The case for ServiceNow

ServiceNow provides an AI platform designed for business transformation by connecting people, data, and devices through cloud-based workflow software. The company serves approximately 8,700 enterprise customers, with a growing segment of business generated from the public sector. Strategic partners include Amazon, Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL), Microsoft, and Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA). The rapid adoption of tech stocks across regulated industries has helped fuel its expansion.
